newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Brazzaville quiet ahead of truce deadline.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville quiet ahead of truce deadline.

text.p: Guns fell silent in the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville on Monday, ahead of an anticipated midnight (2300 GMT) start of a truce, following an outbreak of shooting at nightfall, witnesses said.

"In principle the military should have given instructions for a ceasefire to come into force," one source close to mediation efforts told Reuters in the Democratic Republic of the Congo capital Kinshasa across the Congo River.

President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso put their names to the truce at the weekend to halt over a month of bloody political and ethnic clashes but there has been confusion over the timing.
U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who helped negotiate the truce proposed by Gabon's veteran president, Omar Bongo, said on Sunday it should start at midnight on Monday.
The sound of mortar and heavy machinegun fire were heard across the river in Kinshasa at and after nightfall on Monday.

"There was some sporadic shooting during the day, but until the shelling started it has been relatively calm compared to recent days," said an aid worker returning from Brazzaville. The evening shooting subsided later.
A mediation committee under Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas met earlier on Monday.

The bloody showdown in the capital of the oil-producing former French colony began on June 5 when soldiers surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militias ahead of a now-postponed July 27 presidential election.
The clashes and indiscriminate shellfire have killed hundreds of people, many of them civilians, medical workers say.
Lissouba's spokesman Gregoire Lefouba had said the truce would begin at midnight on Sunday.
Sahnoun has said talks would take place in Gabon's capital Libreville on Tuesday or Wednesday on national reconciliation and creating an environment for elections some time over the next two months.
Plans are taking shape for a U.N.-sponsored, mainly African peacekeeping force.
Diplomats said Bongo was due to send a plane to Brazzaville for representatives of the two sides.
Lissouba's mandate expires at the end of August. He says the constitution allows a 90-day extension to organise elections. Sassou demands a national salvation government.
Lissouba, Sassou and Kolelas, whose militia has kept out of the latest fighting, planned to contest the July 27 election.
Kolelas's militia was at the heart of similar political and ethnic clashes that killed at least 2,000 people in Brazzaville after a disputed 1993 parliamentary election.
